chief_complaint: shortness of breath, expiratory wheezing, and dry cough
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with shortness of breath, expiratory wheezing, and dry cough. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she might be having a bad allergic reaction to dust after cleaning her college dorm room.
concerns: She is worried that her breathing will get so tight during her upcoming final exams that she won't be able to finish them.
expectations: She hopes to get an inhaler or cough medicine to quickly open up her chest so she can study tonight.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Asthma Exacerbation is essential for appropriate diagnostic workup and treatment.
Clinical history, severity assessment, and targeted testing must be interpreted together rather than relying on one symptom alone.
Assess severity objectively with vital signs, oxygen saturation, and peak expiratory flow where feasible.
Management should follow local pathways and account for patient-specific comorbidity and clinical severity.
diagnostic_clues: Chief complaint: shortness of breath, expiratory wheezing, and dry cough

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with shortness of breath, expiratory wheezing, and dry cough. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/examination findings: Perform focused examination, vital-sign assessment, and diagnosis-specific investigations.
common_misconceptions: Assuming a mild or atypical presentation rules out Asthma Exacerbation.
Relying on a single normal test result to prematurely exclude serious pathology.
Equating transient symptom improvement with resolution of the underlying condition.
Failing to consider clinically important alternative diagnoses.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before appropriate assessment.
Starting treatment without considering contraindications, interactions, or organ function.
Ignoring critical warning signs: Unable to speak full sentences or silent chest.
management_principles: Assess severity objectively with vital signs, oxygen saturation, and peak expiratory flow where feasible.
Give inhaled short-acting bronchodilator promptly; add systemic corticosteroids for moderate or severe exacerbations.
Escalate immediately for life-threatening features or inadequate response to initial treatment.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: shortness of breath, expiratory wheezing, and dry cough

A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with shortness of breath, expiratory wheezing, and dry cough. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Asthma Exacerbation.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute wheeze and breathlessness, with asthma exacerbation possible but not yet established because there is no documented prior asthma diagnosis. Assess urgently for severity and alternative causes including anaphylaxis, infection, pneumothorax, and pulmonary embolism when clinically indicated.
reference_soap.plan: Check vital signs, oxygen saturation, work of breathing, and peak flow where feasible. Provide oxygen and repeated inhaled bronchodilator treatment according to local acute-asthma protocol; a clinician should decide whether systemic corticosteroids are indicated after severity assessment. Send for emergency assessment immediately for hypoxaemia, inability to speak full sentences, drowsiness, cyanosis, silent chest, or inadequate response. Once stable, confirm or exclude asthma with objective testing and provide an ICS-containing long-term regimen if diagnosed.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Asthma Exacerbation
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Asthma Exacerbation
Implement severity-based, clinician-directed management while arranging objective confirmation of asthma after the acute episode

teaching.diagnosis: Acute wheeze and breathlessness; possible asthma exacerbation
teaching.one_liner: Acute worsening of asthma symptoms with wheeze, cough, breathlessness, and variable airflow obstruction.
red_flags: Unable to speak full sentences or silent chest
Drowsiness, cyanosis, or poor response to reliever

must_ask.objective: Wheeze and dyspnea onset with trigger identification
must_ask.say: When did the wheezing and breathlessness start, and did anything seem to trigger it, like allergens or exercise?

must_ask.objective: Personal and family history of asthma or atopy
must_ask.say: Have you been diagnosed with asthma before, or does anyone in your family have asthma or allergies?

must_ask.objective: Inhaler use and rescue medication response
must_ask.say: Do you use an inhaler, and does it help relieve your symptoms?

must_ask.objective: Severity red flags: speech, accessory muscle use, peak flow
must_ask.say: Are you able to speak in full sentences, or does it feel like you can't get enough air?

must_ask.objective: Prior exacerbation history and hospitalization risk
must_ask.say: Have you ever needed to go to the hospital or been on steroids for your breathing before?

history.answer: I've been feeling short of breath with this whistling sound whenever I breathe out, and I have a dry cough that's been getting worse.
It started gradually about three days ago, but it has definitely worsened over the last twenty-four hours.
I notice the breathlessness mostly when walking up stairs or hurrying across campus, but right now I feel slightly tight even sitting still.
It has been fairly steady since yesterday, though it definitely gets worse late at night and early in the morning.
I had a couple of milder episodes of chest tightness after catching a cold in the past, but nothing ever felt this severe.
Dust seems to make it much worse, especially when I was cleaning out my closet two days ago, and cold air also triggers the wheezing.
Yes, I can clearly hear and feel a high-pitched whistling noise in my chest, especially as I exhale.
It's been a dry, hacking cough without any phlegm or thick mucus.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweating.
My chest feels tight and constricted like a band around it, but I don't have any sharp, stabbing pain when I take a deep breath.
No heart pounding, dizziness, or lightheadedness, and I have never passed out.
No, I haven't coughed up any blood at all.
I woke up around 3 AM coughing and feeling tight in my chest, but I don't need extra pillows to sleep flat.
No, I haven't had any swelling in my legs or feet, and my weight has not changed.
No swelling or pain in either calf, and I haven't had any surgery, prolonged bed rest, or long travel recently.
I feel generally tired because it takes extra effort to breathe, but I don't have pale skin, heavy menstrual bleeding, or dark stools.
I feel a bit anxious because it's difficult to breathe, but I don't have any tingling around my lips or numbness in my fingers.
No hives, itchy skin rash, or facial and lip swelling, and I didn't eat any unusual foods or get an insect bite.
I have never been diagnosed with asthma or prescribed an inhaler, so I haven't used any breathing medications.
I can manage full sentences, though I need to pause for breath if I try to speak too fast.
No, I have never been hospitalized, admitted to an ICU, or visited the emergency room for breathing trouble.
I thought maybe I was having a severe allergic reaction to all the dust from cleaning out our dorm room.
I'm really worried that this wheezing will flare up during my final exams next week and make me fail.
I was hoping you could give me an inhaler or some medicine to clear my chest so I can get back to studying tonight.
I have no history of major medical illnesses, though I had mild eczema as a child and get occasional seasonal nasal allergies.
I have never had any operations and I have never stayed in a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or herbal supplements.
I do not take aspirin, ibuprofen, beta-blocker blood pressure pills, or any other pain relievers.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
My mother has asthma and seasonal allergies, but there is no family history of blood clots or heart disease.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic vapes.
I drink alcohol socially on occasion, perhaps a beer once or twice a month.
I am a university student living in a college dormitory, with no pets, mold issues, or chemical dust exposures.
My last period began two weeks ago and my cycles are regular every 28 days; I am not sexually active and cannot be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, temperature 36.7°C.
Alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences with mild respiratory effort, without cyanosis of the lips or nail bed clubbing.
Symmetrical chest wall expansion with slightly prolonged expiration, without accessory muscle retractions or chest wall tenderness.
Normal resonant percussion notes bilaterally across all lung fields.
Bilateral diffuse expiratory wheezes throughout both lung fields, with no crackles or stridor.
Regular heart rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Internal jugular venous pulsation is not elevated.
No peripheral pitting edema noted in either lower extremity.
Both calves are symmetric in circumference without swelling, redness, warmth, or tenderness on palpation.
